Freewill Offering
FREE-wil AW-fer-ing
noun phrase (Levitical law / worship / covenant giving)
Old English frēo (free, at liberty) + willa (will, desire) + Old French offrande (offering, oblation), from Latin offerenda (things to be offered), from offerre (to offer, present); the compound names the voluntary, un-commanded gift presented to the LORD above and beyond what the law specifically required; its Hebrew base is nedābāh (נְדָבָה), from nādab (to offer willingly, to volunteer).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The freewill offering is the Levitical category for any sacrifice offered voluntarily — not in response to a vow, not on a commanded feast day, not as atonement for sin — but from the pure impulse of a willing heart. Its Hebrew name nedābāh derives from the root nādab (to volunteer, to give willingly), which appears in Exodus 35:29 describing the construction of the tabernacle: “The children of Israel brought a freewill offering to the LORD, all the men and women whose hearts were willing to bring material for all kinds of work.” The word “willing” here is the same root — the freewill offering is what willing hearts give.

The Levitical regulations for the freewill offering (Lev 22:18–23) specify that it must be a perfect animal but allow for minor blemishes disqualifying animals from vow-based offerings — indicating a gracious standard appropriate to a gift freely given. The freewill offering is accepted in the spirit of its giving rather than measured by absolute perfection.

The Psalmist extends the concept to the offering of words: “Accept, I pray, the freewill offerings of my mouth, O LORD” (Ps 119:108). The voluntary sacrifice of praise, prayer, and profession — the lips' tribute freely given — is encompassed by the same covenant category as the Levitical animal. Ezra 1:4 captures the returning exiles' freewill offerings for the temple rebuilding: the genre spans history and testaments.

Webster 1828 Definition

FREEWILL OFFERING: the Levitical category (nedābāh) for a voluntary sacrifice presented to the LORD from a willing heart, not commanded by law or bound by a vow; extended in the Psalms to encompass verbal offerings of praise and prayer (Ps 119:108) and in the NT to the grace-enabled voluntary giving of the believer (2 Cor 9:7).

FREEWILL OFFERING, noun phrase. In the Levitical system, a voluntary sacrifice presented to the LORD independently of any legal requirement or vow — the pure gift of a willing heart.

Hebrew nedābāh (נְדָבָה), from nādab (to offer willingly, to volunteer); the root also generates nedib (a willing, noble person) — freewill giving is an expression of nobility of character.

The Levitical regulations (Lev 22:18–23) distinguish the freewill offering from the votive offering by degree of perfection required: the freewill offering may have minor blemishes not permitted in vow-offerings, a concession to the voluntariness of the gift.

Paul's principle in 2 Cor 9:7 — “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” — is the NT application of the freewill-offering principle: the Spirit-enabled willing heart is the new-covenant equivalent of nedābāh.

Key Scripture

Ex 35:29 — "The children of Israel brought a freewill offering to the LORD, all the men and women whose hearts were willing to bring material for all kinds of work which the LORD, by the hand of Moses, had commanded to be done."

Ps 119:108 — "Accept, I pray, the freewill offerings of my mouth, O LORD, and teach me Your judgments."

Lev 22:21 — "And whoever offers a sacrifice of a peace offering to the LORD, to fulfill his vow, or a freewill offering from the cattle or the sheep, it must be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no defect in it."

Ezra 1:4 — "And whoever is left in any place where he dwells, let the men of his place help him with silver and gold, with goods and livestock, besides the freewill offerings for the house of God which is in Jerusalem."

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel's transactional theology of giving — seed-faith, tithe-as-investment, giving to get — is the direct antithesis of the freewill offering's theology: giving as voluntary, covenant-loving, joyful tribute to a God whose love is not purchased. The gift becomes a spiritual transaction rather than a willing oblation.

expand to see more

Word-Faith and prosperity-gospel teaching (Kenneth Copeland, Creflo Dollar, Joel Osteen) reframes giving as a covenant seed planted to harvest a financial return — “giving to get.” This is not a distortion of the freewill offering; it is its replacement with an alien theology. The freewill offering in Leviticus is given because the heart is willing, not because the giver calculates a return. Exodus 35's willing-hearted givers bring their gold, silver, and fine linen to the tabernacle out of love for the God who redeemed them from Egypt — not because Moses promised them a hundred-fold return. The motivation of willing love and the motivation of calculated gain are incompatible.

A subtler corruption in mainstream evangelicalism treats giving primarily through the lens of the commanded tithe (10%, Mal 3:10), using the tithe as a floor that satisfies the obligation. The freewill offering's category is explicitly beyond-tithe, beyond-vow, beyond-commanded-feast — it is the overflow of a heart that gives not because it must but because it wants to. The Macedonian churches of 2 Cor 8:1–5 gave out of their extreme poverty, “begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part” — the spirit of freewill offering recognizing no floor and no ceiling, only the willing heart responsive to the grace it has received.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nedābāh from nādab (to volunteer willingly); the root word for freewill giving is also the root for nobility of character — the generous, voluntary heart is the biblical image of the noble person.

expand to see more

Hebrew nādab (נָדַב) — to offer voluntarily, to act willingly, to be moved by generosity; the verbal root from which nedābāh (freewill offering) and nādīb (generous, noble) derive; willing giving and noble character share the same root

Hebrew nedābāh (נְדָבָה) — a freewill offering, a voluntary gift; appears 26 times in the OT; sometimes rendered “willing offering” or “voluntary offering” in modern translations but always conveying the same root: given from within, not required from without

Levitical taxonomy: the freewill offering (nedābāh) was typically a peace offering (zebah shelāmīm) presented outside of the commanded feast occasions; it could also take the form of a grain or drink offering

NT parallel: Greek hekousios (ἑκούσιος) — voluntary, willing; Philemon 14 uses it of service done freely rather than by compulsion; and prothymia (προθυμία) — readiness of mind, eagerness — is Paul's NT term for the freewill-offering spirit (2 Cor 8:11–12)

Usage

"The tabernacle construction in Exodus 35–36 is the paradigm case of freewill giving in the OT: the people gave “all the men and women whose hearts were willing” (Ex 35:29), and they gave so abundantly that Moses had to restrain them — “the people are bringing much more than enough for the service of the work” (Ex 36:5–6). The wilderness church's giving exceeded the demand. This is the spirit of freewill offering at full pitch: not measured giving calibrated to a commanded percentage but overflowing giving from hearts so glad in the covenant that the question “how much must I give?” does not arise."

"The Psalter extends freewill offering to the lips: Ps 119:108 asks the LORD to accept “the freewill offerings of my mouth.” The words of Torah-meditation, praise, and prayer are offered to God as a voluntary tribute of the tongue. This extension is not metaphorical but a genuine expansion of the category: the new-covenant worshiper who brings the sacrifice of praise to God (Heb 13:15 — “the fruit of lips that acknowledge His name”) is presenting a freewill offering of the mouth in the spirit of Ps 119:108."

"The Reformed tradition's theology of giving flows directly from the freewill offering's root meaning. John Calvin's commentary on 2 Cor 9:7 (“God loves a cheerful giver”) emphasizes that the word hilaros (cheerful) indicates genuine interior gladness rather than grudging compliance: “He does not merely praise liberality, but requires that it be voluntary and cheerful.” The covenant God does not need our gifts; He calls for the willing heart that the gift expresses."
